exports.1: We're sending Doña Ester and two of the old winch mechanics, who have spent forty years diagnosing cable machinery by ear alone and can tell you blindfolded whether a hum is a bearing, a transformer, or a building resonating in sympathy with something three streets away. If they find nothing, they will at least tell you what note it is — and then we ship you enough second-hand street organs tuned to that note that the ambience becomes municipal property, with a budget, a caretaker, and a proper channel for complaints.
exports.3: Answer it. We'll send a portable Aldis lamp, a full fuel can and a retired harbour pilot who reads lamp-rhythm the way other people read handwriting, to sit out on the point every clear night, repeat the pattern back exactly once when it comes, and write down what the light does next — three greetings left hanging isn't caution, it's bad manners.
exports.4: We'll ship four hundred metres of pontoon duckboard — the same bolt-together decking our stall-holders use to trade on a forty-degree hill — plus the carpenters who assemble it in a morning, so the market simply rises a foot and keeps selling straight through the four days. And we'll paint a gauge up the wall at the low end, marked and dated by year, so that in a decade the water isn't a failure, it's a record, and the children can argue about which flood was the famous one.
exports.5: Take the stevedore's plate and make it yours in lamb: one pan, potatoes cut thick and fried in dripping, meat and onion collapsed over the top, two eggs, four forks, no side dishes and no reservation. We'll send you the cook who has made nothing else for nineteen years to stand in a kitchen of your choosing for a month, and the only two rules that matter — it is eaten out of the pan by people who are touching elbows, and it is available at three in the morning, or that magazine was right about you.
exports.7: Our fruit terminal handles an entire southern stone-fruit season, which means that this week our cold rooms are empty and eighty packers are painting their own houses out of boredom. Give us three days' notice and we'll put forty reefer containers on your siding with the crews already inside them — your plums leave as fruit, not as jam and not as brandy, and land in a hemisphere where it is February, it is dark at four, and a fresh plum sells for what a bottle of anything sells for.
exports.8: Don't clear the avenue, obstruct it. We'll ship the staggered zinc-and-timber baffles our hill streets use, set at an angle every thirty metres and alternating sides so the wind loses its run-up and has to zigzag like the rest of us — and with them four kilometres of knotted rope handrail and the ironmonger's crew to bolt it at hand height down both pavements, because dignity is mostly a question of having something to hold.
exports.10: Your residents are not counting spaces, they are counting how far they will be made to walk carrying something heavy in weather, and no study has ever measured that. Valparaíso has almost no parking and almost no argument about it, because we put the money into fifteen funiculars instead — so pick one hard hill or one long street, build a lift that runs free and runs late and is worth riding for its own sake, and let people leave the car wherever it lands. We'll send the engineers who keep our hundred-year-old ascensores turning, and 'where do I park' quietly becomes 'anywhere, obviously.'
exports.11: Stop replacing the trees; nothing with a trunk that thin has ever beaten salt. We'll send two crates of rooted bougainvillea, six hundred aloe pups and a sack of ice-plant cuttings torn off our own cliff faces — all of it grows in rubble on salt spray and none of it wants anything from you — planted at the foot of the stakes you have maintained so beautifully, so that in two years the stakes are trellises and the promenade is magenta from one end to the other.
exports.12: Our port has run a night crèche since the docks went round the clock: one warm room by the gate, eleven cots, a levy the employers pay per night-shift worker rather than per child, and a standing rule that the children sleep there and are carried home asleep at seven. We'll lend you, for a full season, the two women who have worked the ten-to-seven shift for a decade and the two pages of rules that actually matter — and take that rota out of the locker and put it on the payroll, because goodwill is a wage somebody is quietly not being paid.
exports.13: We volunteer. First we send the trophy — an appalling object, a metre of welded ship's brass on a plinth of harbour timber, too heavy for one man to carry and too ugly to display without an explanation — and a signed fixture, first Sunday of every March, alternating ports, in perpetuity. Then we send the grievance: some years ago one of your vessels took a record off us under circumstances we have described as theft ever since, and by the second match your own side will believe it too.
exports.14: We sit on a fault line, so every building we own is held up by something that was meant to be temporary in 1906 — the only real difference is that we stopped apologising for it and moved it into the budget under maintenance. We'll send four shipwrights and the yard foreman who reframe our roofs in laminated timber built to move rather than resist, Oregon pine enough for a span your size, and one piece of advice: name the scaffolding, give it a plaque and a line item, and it will outlast all three permits and very probably you.
exports.15: Fish soup, at four in the morning, from a counter that shuts at nine and does not open again until four. We'll send the whole kit — the two vast pots, the cook who has done nothing else since he was nineteen, and the rule that every man gets the same bowl at the same price with bread and a glass of white wine and nobody insults him by suggesting coffee — because someone coming off nights isn't starting his day, he's ending it, and he should be fed like it's dinner.

answers.1: Swimming in the sea. I have lived my entire life eighty metres above it and I have been in it twice, neither time on purpose.
answers.2: The Reina Victoria funicular, upward. Ninety seconds, costs almost nothing, and at the top you turn round and the bay does the thing it does — then we walk down through the stairs and get comprehensively lost, which is the actual tour.
answers.4: For. Loudly, unfashionably, permanently for — and I have been told my ceviche is aggressive about it, which I take as the compliment it was not.
answers.5: A tide table from 1971 with my father's notes down the margins about which mornings were worth getting out of bed for. Roughly half of them say no.
answers.7: Tuesday, seven o'clock, and nobody wants anything from me. I walk down from the office rather than take the car, buy fish on the way from the man who overcharges me and knows I know, and cook it slightly badly with the radio doing a football match I have no stake in. There is usually a dog on the step — never the same dog — that waits to be fed and then leaves without ceremony. Window open, in bed by ten. Tuesday is the one night the port unloads quietly.
answers.8: Not my predecessor, who taught me mainly what a closed door sounds like. Señora Fuentes, thirty years on the newspaper kiosk at the bottom of the hill, who knew every complaint in this city a week before it reached my desk and, more usefully, which ones would go away on their own.
answers.9: My sister. She has never once been impressed by anything I've done, which is precisely how I know when a thing is actually good.
answers.11: A brass ship's bell bolted to the corner of it, which I did not install and cannot remove without a carpenter and a formal request. My assistant rings it when I have been talking too long, and I have yet to find a dignified way to object.
answers.12: Whichever one I can explain faster to somebody standing on a street corner in the wind. If it takes more than two sentences it was never the fine option, I just hadn't noticed yet.
answers.13: The kitchen, which was most of the downstairs of a house on Cerro Cordillera — zinc walls, one window. My mother had got a green cheap off the port, so we had that green in the kitchen and the neighbours had the same green on their boat, and neither of us ever mentioned it. The table had one short leg with a fold of newspaper under it that was changed perhaps twice in my whole childhood. From the window you could see three cranes, and by twelve I could tell from the noise alone whether a ship was loading or leaving.
answers.14: The upper station of a funicular that hasn't run since 2011. Nobody has cleared out the operator's chair, the window still faces the right way, and there is no telephone in it.
answers.15: A cueca on an accordion, played slightly too fast by a man who fully expects to be paid for it. I would prefer a brass section, obviously, but one works with the city one has.
answers.16: A tin of paint from a colour we stopped using in 1998. It has been solid for twenty years and has followed me through three offices, but if one house on that hill ever needs touching up I would like to be able to say what the colour was called.
